Reviews 375 The central figure of the novel, Volodia Pukhov, however, does not finld a solution for his problems. A painter-conformist, he chooses socially- approved subjects and techniques for hiis canvases of prominent factory man- agers, smiling pioneers, and optimistic workers. He has money and recogni- tion, but he knows that he prostituted his art, that he failed as an artist, and he is envious of Saburov, who is starving in obscurity but does not compro- mise and asserts himself as a creator. This opposition of Pukhov and Sabul- rov as representatives, on the one hand, of the official but artificial art that leads to potboilers and, on the other, semiclandestine true art that condemns to loneliness and misery was interpreted by Russian readers as a bold de- mand for a complete revision of existing aesthetic requirements. In other areas Ehrenburg also dealt with forbidden themes. For the first time a fiction writer mentioned things that had passed in an awesome silence under Stalin: Vera Sherer speaks of the famous "doctors' plot" against Soviet leaders, and alludes to official anti-Semitism; we learn that Koroteev's stepfather, Vyrl- bin, had been arrested and exiled during the purges; this victim of Stalinist terror comes home after fifteen years in a concentration camp; Sokolovsky is open to slander and may get in trouble because his former wife lives in Belgium; Zhuravlev, Lena's husband whom she finally leaves, is a limited bureaucrat who sacrifices his workers in order to fulfill quotas and receive the praise of the ministry; and the life of Volodia's mistress, the little actress Tanechka, is full of humiliations and indignities, just as in prerevolutionary Russia. All these traits and descriptions seemed very exciting to the Russian readers of the early fifties. The topical and political symbolism of the novel redeemed its obvious artistic shortcomings: it had no depth of characteriza- tion, its structure was loose, its style journalistic, with the sharp black an(d white strokes so typical of Ehrenburg's manner, and from a purely literary standpoint it was by no means a remarkable piece of writing. But "The. Thaw" (its sequel is much less convincing even as a story) should not be judged apart from its historical context. It has meaning and value as at document of a period and as evidence of changes in the Russian scene aftei- Stalin's death. Yetn many critics have been too preoccupied with the political implications of a novel that Premier Khruishchev has made "recom- nended reading," while paying lip service to the literary merits of the work. What is Ivan Denisovich's place in literature? Is the story to become another political episode like Dudintsev's Not by B-ead Alone? Is it just a captivating but short-lived vignette? One finds in the craftsmanship of Solzhenitsyn's style the answer to these questions. Solzhenitsyn's chief aim is to portray a human character, to show the "dialectics of the soul." It is true that, so far as external factors are concerned, Ivan Denisovich can be called Everyman. His situation is a typical one, his life has been less colorful than those of some of his fellow prisoners, and his personality lacks dramatic tLraits which might make him a "romantic" hero. But Ivan Denisovich has a whole spiritual universe of his own, and it is the author's aim to depict this universe that determines the choice of episodes and, in fact, the whole structure of the novel. Through the technique of the skaz, events and people are seen throulgh Ivan's eyes and are described in his vital, flavorful language-a composite of concentration camp slang, peasant speech, and individual jargon. In the skaz, two manners of presentation in addition to dialogue must be distin- guished: they might be labeled the narrative and the dramatic. Solzhenit- syn uses the first one to present an orderly narrative, sustaining with great artistic skill a tone of understatement. Against this flowing rhythm certain passages or statements crucial to the psychological portrait of Ivan Deniso- vich stand out strikingly and have a resonant effect. Example: NARRATIVE VOICE: Iii warmer weather everybody in the column talked, Iio niattcr how mtuch the escort might shout at them. But today every prisoner hunched his shouLlders, hid behind the back of the mian in front of hiiii, an-d pluinged into his own thoughts ... DRAMATIC VOICE: ..The thoughts of a prisoner-they're not free, either. They keep returning to the same ttiings. A single idea keeps stirring ... (p. 47; translation by Parker). It is on stylistic points such as these-subtle yet so vital to the litelary distinctiveness of the book-that Mr. Hayward's translation falters. Pre- occupied with rendering the flavor of a smoothly flowNTing skaz, he seems not to distinguish the two tones, and the phrases so dramatized in the original are submerged in the monotone of the narrative. Witness the translation of the same passage: Everyone talks in the column when it's warmer, no miatter how miuch they're sholuted at. But today everyone was bent forward, hiding behind the back of the man in front and thinking his own thoughts. Even a prisoner's thoughts weren't free but kept cominig back to the same thing, kept tuirning the same things over again ... (pp. 44-45; translation by Hayward and Hingley). Parker follows the syntactical pattern of the original more closely than Hayward, and thus the two voices pulsating in the skaz come through more clearly. On the other hand, Mr. Hayward's use of vivid slang and colloqui- alisms does draw the reader into the protagonist's frame of mind, as well as into the sights and sounds of the dreary island in the Siberian wasteland. It seems, however, that the vulgarism of Ivan's speech has somewhat colored All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

Reviews 377 the translator's interpretation of his character, and the singularly poeti' inner quality of Ivan's meditations is weakened in the translation. Mr. Parker also uses slang, yet he does not have the same compulsion to spice every sentence of the story with it. Thus the reader is able to concen- trate on the psychological meaning rather than on verbal play, and senses Ivan's deeper, lyrical moods. Unfortunately, though the slang is there, Parker has a tendency to drift off into a too civilized language, destroying the freshness of Ivan's vision. For example: The moon rode high now. As high again, and it would be at its zenith. The sky Was greenish-white; the rare stars shone brilliantly ... (p. 150; Parker). Contrast this with Hayward's more colloquial, almost Hemingway-like rendering: The moon was real high up now. A little ma-ore and it'd be all the way up. The sky wvas pale-and sort of greenish. The stars were bright, and there weren't manly of them p. (P. 197; Hayward and Hingley). It is difficult to make an uncompromising statement about the relative merits of the two translations. Mr. Hayward's is more creative and capti- vating from the point of view of language; Mr. Parker's is more sensitive to the subtle transitions of mood. A synthesis of the two could produce an excellent translation. A great deal more could be said about the style and structure of a novel. Language is only one of the literary devices which create a complex inner x,\orld of a person troubled by a serious conflict with a hostile environment. In sum, Solzhenitsyn's style, skillfully interwoven as it is with the conten-t, raises Ivan Denisovich's story high above the level of a mere ideological weapon, giving it flesh and blood. Long after the repercussions of the Stalin era will have ended, the drama of Ivan Denisovich should still stir the hearts of readers. Harvard University IRINA H. SHAPIRO MARIA KUNCEWICZ (ed.), The Modern Polish Mind: An Anthology. Boston and Toronto: Little, Brown, 1962. viii + 440 pp. $8.50. Mlrs. Kuncewicz' extensive and well-conceived anthology is one of the maost welcome publications in recent years. A neatly proportioned variety of very recent short pieces, stories, and essays, numbering over forty, are classed into four ingenious, comprehensive groups, en-titled respectively: "What Polish Writers Remember," "How They See Life," "What They Believe," "Their Humor." One could, of course, argue that humor might-and it indeed does-enter into the other three groups; and one could also prefer to see within the volume certain examples of the contemnporary Polish mind whiclh have been sacrificed for others. What counts is that Mrs. Kuncewicz' selec- tion possesses an anthological character and gives a realistic picture of tlle subject. The translations, if not uniform, are on the whole readable. My chief criticism is of the introduction, which is all too brief.
